paragraphs.text: The drug does not change the bacteria. In a large infection, a few bacteria already carry a resistance gene... The bacteria become resistant, not the patient's body.

paragraphs.at: What a cell must block, para 1
paragraphs.text: An antibiotic is a molecule that kills bacteria or stops their growth... penicillin binds the enzymes that build the cell wall.

paragraphs.at: What a cell must block, para 2
paragraphs.text: A resistance gene is a gene, changed by mutation or received from another bacterium, that blocks this. It works in one of four ways:
Destroy the drug / Change the target / Pump the drug out / Keep the drug out
excess: One DNA letter change in the rpoB gene

paragraphs.at: What a cell must block, MIC paragraph
paragraphs.text: Each way means the cell needs more drug to stop it. The lowest concentration ... is its MIC ... (Illustrative values.)

paragraphs.at: Resistant cells are there before the drug, para 1
paragraphs.text: A given resistance mutation happens about once per 10⁸ cell divisions ... Growing to that size took about 10¹⁰ divisions, so expect
leap: Growing to that size took about 10¹⁰ divisions: the reason (going from 1 cell to N cells takes about N−1 divisions) is not given
excess: (order of magnitude; real values range from about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹⁰)

paragraphs.text: 10¹⁰ × 10⁻⁸ = 100 resistance mutations, before anyone gives a drug.
Early mutants have divided since, so there are at least 100 resistant cells. Compare a small infection of 10⁶ cells...
The drug stops the susceptible cells, and the immune system clears them.
The resistant cells keep dividing... (A weakened patient clears fewer.)
A doubling is one round in which every cell divides once. 100 cells need 27 doublings to reach 10¹⁰ again (2²⁷ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁸)...
leap: (2²⁷ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁸): the reader has to multiply by the starting 100 cells to get 10¹⁰, and the text never says so
excess: A doubling is one round in which every cell divides once.

paragraphs.text: The infection returns, and now almost every cell is resistant.

paragraphs.at: The drug selects them, para after list
paragraphs.text: This is selection: the drug did not make resistant cells, it removed everything else.

paragraphs.at: The drug selects them, Luria–Delbrück paragraph
paragraphs.text: How do we know the drug did not cause the change? ... They found 11 cultures with 0 and one with 107...
unresolved: with a virus as the killing agent
leap: so the "drug causes it" idea predicts most cultures between 5 and 18: the text never says where the 5–18 range comes from

paragraphs.text: A cell does not have to wait for its own rare mutation. A plasmid is a small circle of DNA... horizontal gene transfer...
Plasmids carry complete working genes... The same plasmid gene turns up in different species, and one plasmid often carries several resistance genes at once.
leap: The same plasmid gene turns up in different species: the text doesn't say this is evidence of transfer, or what it is meant to show

paragraphs.text: Resistant cells take over only while the drug is present. Without the drug, resistance often has a fitness cost...
Suppose resistant cells grow 5% slower... Plasmids also persist.
leap: Plasmids also persist.: no reason is given

paragraphs.text: Large infections are the risk, because they hold resistant cells before treatment.
Two drugs with independent targets need two mutations in one cell... This fails if one plasmid or one pump resists both drugs: then about 100 cells survive again.
resistance genes come first, by chance or from other bacteria. The drug removes the competitors, and the resistant cells multiply.
Persister cells... transformation and transduction... SOS response... biofilms.

question.text: How do bacteria come to resist an antibiotic: does the drug cause the change, or does it select bacteria that were already resistant?
question.known_at: Title and the bold lead paragraph
question.result_stated: Yes, in the lead: "The drug does not change the bacteria... The drug removes their competitors, and the resistant bacteria multiply."

reply.motive: Neither motive is stated outright. A reason to care is only implied, by "The infection returns, and now almost every cell is resistant." There is no stated reason for the counting approach, though the arithmetic in "10¹⁰ × 10⁻⁸ = 100 resistance mutations, before anyone gives a drug" makes the case by example.
reply.close: Yes: "In short: resistance genes come first, by chance or from other bacteria. The drug removes the competitors, and the resistant cells multiply."
reply.recap: A big infection already holds about a hundred resistant bacteria before treatment, from random mutation or genes passed between bacteria, and the drug just clears away everything else so they take over.
reply.strongest: 'Resistant cells are there before the drug': the 10¹⁰ × 10⁻⁸ = 100 calculation, together with the Luria–Delbrück paragraph that tests the idea.
reply.weakest: 'Genes from other bacteria', para 2: the facts in it (the same gene in different species, several genes on one plasmid) are stated without saying what they show.
suggestions: Say where 5–18 comes from (Poisson spread: about mean ± 2√mean).
Explain that a virus can infect and kill bacteria (a bacteriophage).
Add one sentence on why resistance matters: treatment fails and the patient relapses.
Say why plasmids persist without the drug, or cut that sentence.
